findings.title: Cleanup registers removal of a non-existent IDP alias ("alias") instead of the created one
findings.body: `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` uses the literal string "alias" rather than the alias actually created (`idp-alias-<i>`, and `idp-alias-20` on line 425). Consequently (a) the cleanup call targets a provider that never exists, so it will fail/throw at teardown, and (b) the realm-level providers created by this test (`idp-alias-0`..`idp-alias-9`, which are not linked to an organization and therefore not removed together with the organizations) are left behind in the shared test realm. Any other test in the class that counts identity providers or login-eligible providers can then fail depending on JUnit method ordering. The alias must be captured in a local final variable and used in the cleanup lambda.

findings.title: Login-cache invalidation on update is decided from the organization-aware wrapper, so it depends on transient organization state
findings.body: `update()` passes `idpById` (obtained from `getById()`, which returns the anonymous `IdentityProviderModel` subclass created by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel`) into `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns `false` whenever the linked organization (or the organization provider for the realm) is disabled, even though the stored IDP row is enabled. As a result `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` can evaluate to `false` for an IDP that *is* present in the cached login ID sets (the DB query behind `getForLogin` only filters on the IDP's own `enabled` flag, not on the organization state). In that situation an update that really removes the IDP from the login set (e.g. setting `hideOnLogin=true` or clearing `kc.org.broker.public`) takes the `!test(original) && !test(updated)` early return and does *not* invalidate `*.idp.login.*`. Because enabling/disabling an organization (a group attribute change) also does not invalidate those keys, after the organization is re-enabled `getForLogin` keeps returning the now hidden/non-public provider - `getForLogin` never re-applies the login predicate to the re-resolved models, and callers only re-check `isEnabled()`. Note the inconsistency with `remove()`, which correctly uses the unwrapped `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)`; `update()` should likewise use the raw stored model (or compare only the IDP's own fields).

findings.title: New invalidation paths in create()/remove() are only tested for the negative case
findings.body: The test only removes `idp-alias-1` (a disabled provider, i.e. not login-eligible) and only creates `idp-alias-20` with `hideOnLogin=true`, so both assertions verify that the login caches are *not* invalidated. The newly added `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(model)` in `create()` and `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` in `remove()` are therefore never exercised in their positive branch: a regression that drops either call (leaving the login caches stale after adding or deleting a login-eligible broker) would not be caught. Add a case that creates an enabled, non-hidden provider and one that removes a login-eligible provider, and assert the `*.idp.login.*` entries disappear.

findings.title: Search key includes organizationId even for REALM_ONLY, and per-organization entries accumulate without bound
findings.body: The search key is always derived from `organizationId`, but for `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` the delegate ignores `organizationId` entirely (it forces `ORGANIZATION_ID=null`). Any caller invoking `getForLogin(REALM_ONLY, someOrgId)` therefore creates a distinct search key for a logically identical result, and each new key triggers `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` plus a full re-query before being merged back. For `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL`, one cached `IdentityProviderListQuery` per realm accumulates one entry per organization id ever queried, with no bound or pruning, so memory grows with the number of organizations that are used for login. Consider using an empty search key for REALM_ONLY and bounding/keying per-organization results separately.

findings.title: getForLogin now returns providers in non-deterministic order
findings.body: The cached implementation collects internal ids into a `HashSet` and returns `new HashSet<>(...).stream()`, so the order of the returned providers is unspecified and can differ between calls/JVMs. Before this change the stream order followed the underlying query order (realm-level providers first, then organization providers, in the order produced by JPA). Callers that rely on a stable order or that take `findFirst()` on the result will now behave unpredictably; the login page happens to re-sort, but the SPI contract change affects every other consumer. Either preserve ordering (e.g. `LinkedHashSet`/list) or document that the order is undefined.

findings.title: getLoginPredicate dereferences getConfig() which may be null
findings.body: The new predicate does `Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC))` whenever `idp.getOrganizationId() != null`. `IdentityProviderModel.getConfig()` is not guaranteed to be non-null (it can be set to `null` via `setConfig`, e.g. when a representation without a config is converted), so this can throw a `NullPointerException` from `create()`/`update()` in the Infinispan provider, which now calls the predicate on the caller-supplied model. Use a null-safe access (e.g. `idp.getConfig() != null && Boolean.parseBoolean(...)`) or `getConfig().getOrDefault` on a guaranteed map.
